title: Map a Product Entity
description: Create a Product entity mapped to a 'products' table. It should have: an auto-generated Long ID using IDENTITY strategy, a non-nullable name (max 200 chars), a non-nullable price (BigDecimal with 10 precision and 2 scale), a unique SKU (50 chars), an ENUMERATED status stored as STRING, a boolean inStock with default true, and a @Transient displayLabel field.
hints: @Entity marks the class; @Table(name='products') sets the table name
@Id + @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) for the primary key
@Column(nullable = false, length = 200) for the name field
@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) stores the enum name as text, not ordinal
@Transient means the field is not persisted

solution.explanation: Every JPA entity needs @Entity and a no-args constructor (which can be protected to prevent direct instantiation outside the persistence provider). @Table(name) overrides the default table name. @GeneratedValue(strategy = IDENTITY) relies on MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT or PostgreSQL's BIGSERIAL — the DB generates the ID at INSERT time. @Column constraints (nullable, length, precision, scale) are reflected in the DDL generated by Hibernate's schema generation but also serve as documentation. EnumType.STRING is strongly preferred over EnumType.ORDINAL — if you ever add, remove, or reorder enum constants, ORDINAL mapping breaks existing data silently. @Transient keeps the displayLabel out of the database entirely — useful for derived or display-only fields computed at the service layer.

methodSignatures.description: Marks this class as a JPA entity; Hibernate will manage and persist instances
Delegates ID generation to the database's auto-increment mechanism
Stores enum as VARCHAR with the constant name; use over ORDINAL for safety
Excludes the field from all persistence operations

title: SEQUENCE Primary Key with allocationSize
description: Create an Invoice entity using a SEQUENCE generation strategy for its primary key. Configure the sequence with a custom name 'invoice_id_seq' and allocationSize of 50. Explain why SEQUENCE is preferred over IDENTITY for PostgreSQL applications that need batch inserts.
hints: Need both @SequenceGenerator and @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = 'generatorName')
allocationSize = 50 means Hibernate fetches 50 IDs per DB round trip, dramatically reducing calls to the sequence
The @SequenceGenerator annotation can go on the class or the field — field-level is more common

solution.explanation: SEQUENCE strategy is superior to IDENTITY for batch operations. With IDENTITY, Hibernate must fire each INSERT individually and read back the generated ID before it can insert the next row. With SEQUENCE, Hibernate calls nextval('invoice_id_seq') to get the next value from the database sequence. With allocationSize = 50, Hibernate fetches 50 IDs in one round trip and allocates them from memory for the next 50 INSERTs — dramatically reducing database roundtrips during bulk inserts. The sequence in the database must be created with INCREMENT BY 50 to match. This is why allocationSize = 50 is the recommended default for any table that will receive significant write volume. IDENTITY is simpler but limits INSERT throughput.

methodSignatures.description: Defines a sequence generator; name links to @GeneratedValue.generator, sequenceName is the DB object name
Uses the named sequence generator for ID generation
Number of IDs to pre-allocate per DB sequence call; DB sequence INCREMENT BY must match this value

title: Bidirectional OneToMany with Helper Methods
description: Create an Order entity with a bidirectional @OneToMany relationship to OrderItem. Configure proper cascade, orphanRemoval, and LAZY fetching. Implement addItem() and removeItem() helper methods to keep both sides of the relationship in sync.
hints: @OneToMany(mappedBy = 'order', cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
mappedBy points to the field name in OrderItem that holds the foreign key
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = 'order_id', nullable = false) on the OrderItem side
addItem must call both: items.add(item) AND item.setOrder(this) to keep the owning side in sync

solution.explanation: The owning side of a bidirectional relationship is the side with the @JoinColumn — here it's OrderItem (the 'many' side, which holds the foreign key column order_id). mappedBy on the Order side tells JPA it does NOT own the relationship; it's a navigation convenience. Only changes to the owning side are persisted — that's why addItem() must call item.setOrder(this): you must update the owning side for the FK to be written to the database. Without the helper method, you could add an item to order.getItems() but the FK column in order_items would remain null. orphanRemoval = true combined with removeItem() means you never need orderItemRepository.delete() — just remove from the collection and Hibernate handles deletion at flush time.

methodSignatures.description: Non-owning side of the relationship; mappedBy = field name in the owning entity
Owning side; explicitly LAZY to avoid unwanted joins when loading collections of OrderItem
Entities removed from the collection are automatically deleted from the database at flush time

title: ManyToMany with Explicit Join Entity
description: Model a Student-Course enrollment system. Instead of using @ManyToMany directly, create an Enrollment join entity that holds the student, the course, the enrollment date, and the grade. Use @EmbeddedId for the composite key.
hints: @Embeddable on EnrollmentId; it must implement Serializable and override equals/hashCode
@EmbeddedId EnrollmentId id on Enrollment; @ManyToOne @MapsId('studentId') maps the student FK to the embedded id field
new EnrollmentId(studentId, courseId) before creating an Enrollment
OneToMany on Student/Course should be LAZY (default for collections)

solution.explanation: The explicit join entity pattern is superior to pure @ManyToMany when the join table needs extra columns (enrolledDate, grade) or when you need to query enrollments directly. @Embeddable with Serializable is required for composite keys — JPA uses equals/hashCode for identity comparison and entity caching. @MapsId('studentId') links the @ManyToOne relationship to the studentId field inside the embedded ID, so you don't need to manually set enrollment.getId().setStudentId() — it's derived from the Student entity. This pattern also eliminates the N+1 and duplicate-join issues that @ManyToMany with @JoinTable can cause. To find all courses for a student: student.getEnrollments().stream().map(Enrollment::getCourse).collect(toList()).

methodSignatures.description: Marks a class as embeddable; it must implement Serializable for use as a composite key
Marks the field as a composite primary key using an @Embeddable class
Maps the FK of a @ManyToOne to a specific field in the @EmbeddedId class

title: Basic JPQL Queries in a Repository
description: Write JPQL queries in an EmployeeRepository: find by email (exact), find all employees in a given city, find employees with salary above a threshold ordered by salary desc, and count employees by department.
hints: @Query("SELECT e FROM Employee e WHERE e.email = :email") for the email query
Use ORDER BY e.salary DESC in the JPQL string for sorting
GROUP BY in JPQL: SELECT e.department, COUNT(e) FROM Employee e GROUP BY e.department
@Param('paramName') binds the method parameter to the named :paramName in JPQL

solution.explanation: JPQL operates on entity names and field names, not table/column names. 'Employee' in FROM refers to the Java class, not the 'employees' table — this is the key difference from SQL. Named parameters (:email) are strongly preferred over positional parameters (?1) for readability and refactoring safety. The @Param annotation binds the method argument to the named parameter. For the aggregation query, Object[] is the return type when selecting multiple values that don't map to a single entity; index 0 is the department name (String) and index 1 is the count (Long). Alternatively, use interface projections or a DTO constructor expression for type-safe results. Note that countByDepartment() is a custom name — it doesn't follow derived query conventions, which is why @Query is necessary.

methodSignatures.description: Executes the given JPQL query; use @Param to bind parameters
Binds the annotated method parameter to the named :name parameter in the JPQL
JPQL aggregation using entity alias; result mapped to Object[] or DTO projection

title: Fix N+1 with JOIN FETCH
description: You have an Order entity with a LAZY @ManyToOne Customer and a LAZY @OneToMany List<OrderItem>. Write a repository query that loads all pending orders WITH their customer and items in a single query to avoid N+1. Also write a query that finds a single order by ID with all associations loaded.
hints: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer WHERE o.status = 'PENDING'
For loading both customer and items: SELECT DISTINCT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer JOIN FETCH o.items WHERE o.id = :id
Using DISTINCT in JPQL prevents duplicate Order results when joining to a collection
Hibernate might throw MultipleBagFetchException if two List collections are fetched — use Set instead of List for one to avoid this

solution.explanation: JOIN FETCH tells Hibernate to include the association in the SQL JOIN instead of issuing a separate SELECT. Without it, loading 100 pending orders fires 100 additional queries for customers — the classic N+1 problem. DISTINCT in JPQL is essential when JOIN FETCHing a collection: the SQL JOIN multiplies Order rows by the number of items, so without DISTINCT you get duplicate Order objects in the result. Hibernate 6 handles this automatically in many cases, but DISTINCT is still good practice. The MultipleBagFetchException arises when you try to JOIN FETCH two List (Bag) collections simultaneously — Hibernate can't determine the correct multiplication. Fix: change one or both to Set, or use separate queries for each collection. For the two-query approach, call both findOrderWithCustomer and findOrderWithItems and Hibernate will merge them in the first-level cache.

methodSignatures.description: Eager-loads the association via SQL JOIN in the same query; overrides LAZY for this query
Deduplicates parent entities when joining to a collection to avoid repeated rows
Thrown when fetching 2+ List associations simultaneously; fix by using Set or separate queries

title: Derived Query Methods
description: Write derived query methods in a ProductRepository covering various scenarios: find by name (case-insensitive), find by price range, find by category and active status, find top 5 most expensive, check existence by SKU, and count by category.
hints: findByNameContainingIgnoreCase follows the Spring Data naming convention
findByPriceBetween(BigDecimal min, BigDecimal max) for range queries
findByCategoryAndActiveTrue for AND condition with boolean true check
findTop5ByActiveTrueOrderByPriceDesc for top 5 ordering

solution.explanation: Spring Data parses the method name using a DSL: subject (find/count/exists/delete) + criteria (By + conditions). ContainingIgnoreCase generates LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER('%keyword%'). Between generates a BETWEEN clause. AndActiveTrue is shorthand for AND active = true — Spring Data recognizes True and False as boolean value suffixes. Top5 limits results to 5 rows. OrderBy followed by a field name and ASC/DESC adds a SQL ORDER BY. This all happens at startup: Spring Data generates the JPQL at application initialization and throws an exception immediately if a field name doesn't match (fail-fast). The key rule: if the method name exceeds ~60 characters, switch to @Query for readability.

methodSignatures.description: LIKE %value% with case-insensitive comparison
SQL BETWEEN min AND max
Limits result to N rows ordered by the specified field descending

title: @Query with @Modifying and DTO Projection
description: Write three advanced repository methods: 1) a @Modifying @Query to bulk-update product prices by category, 2) a native SQL query, and 3) an interface-based projection that returns only id, name, and price without loading full entities.
hints: @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) + @Transactional + @Query("UPDATE Product p SET p.price = p.price * :factor WHERE p.category = :cat")
For native query: @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY (price * stock_count) DESC LIMIT :limit", nativeQuery = true)
Interface projection: just return the projection interface from a derived or @Query method — Spring generates the implementation
SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.active = true automatically maps to ProductSummary if you declare it as the return type

solution.explanation: @Modifying marks the query as a DML statement (UPDATE/DELETE), not a SELECT. Without it, Spring Data throws an exception. clearAutomatically = true clears the persistence context after execution, preventing stale entity instances from being returned by subsequent finds within the same transaction — important because the bulk UPDATE bypasses the persistence context (entities already loaded into memory won't reflect the new prices until the context is cleared or refreshed). @Transactional is required because DML must run within a transaction. Interface-based projections are zero-config: Spring Data auto-generates a proxy implementing the interface and maps query result columns to getter return values. The AS alias in the @Query JPQL ensures column names match the getter method names after stripping 'get' and lowercasing the first letter.

methodSignatures.description: Marks as DML; clearAutomatically evicts stale entities from the persistence context post-update
Executes raw SQL instead of JPQL; bypasses the JPA entity model
Spring Data generates a dynamic proxy; property names must match query result column aliases

title: @Transactional Propagation — REQUIRES_NEW
description: Implement an order placement service where audit logging must always succeed even if the order placement fails. Use REQUIRES_NEW propagation for the audit method to run in its own independent transaction.
hints: @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW) on logEvent suspends the outer transaction and creates a new one
The REQUIRES_NEW transaction commits immediately when logEvent returns
When the outer transaction rolls back (InsufficientStockException), the audit log's committed data is NOT rolled back
Important: REQUIRES_NEW works only when called from a DIFFERENT Spring bean (not self-invocation)

solution.explanation: REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current (outer) transaction, starts a completely new transaction, executes the method, and commits it before resuming the outer transaction. This makes the audit log durable regardless of what happens in the outer transaction. If inventoryService.reserveStock() throws InsufficientStockException, the outer transaction rolls back — reverting the order save — but the audit log remains committed. Critical caveat: REQUIRES_NEW only works when called through Spring's proxy, meaning the method must be called from a different bean. If OrderService called its own logEvent() method directly (self-invocation), the proxy is bypassed and the annotation is ignored. Always inject AuditService as a separate bean rather than creating a new instance. REQUIRES_NEW is ideal for: audit logs, notification sending, metrics recording — operations that must succeed independently of the business transaction.

methodSignatures.description: Suspends existing transaction, opens a new one; commits independently regardless of outer tx outcome
Default: join existing transaction or create a new one if none exists
Creates a savepoint within the outer transaction; rollback to savepoint on failure, not full outer rollback

title: readOnly = true and Optimistic Locking
description: Demonstrate two features: 1) Mark a service method with @Transactional(readOnly = true) for a read-only product listing, and 2) Add optimistic locking with @Version to a Product entity and handle the OptimisticLockingFailureException in an update service.
hints: @Version on a Long field — Hibernate auto-increments it on every UPDATE and checks it in the WHERE clause
@Transactional(readOnly = true) tells Hibernate to skip dirty checking at flush time
OptimisticLockingFailureException is thrown by Spring Data when the @Version check fails
Catch ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException and either retry or throw a ConcurrentModificationException to the caller

solution.explanation: readOnly = true is a performance optimization for read-only transactions. Hibernate builds a snapshot of every loaded entity for dirty checking at flush time — with readOnly = true, this is skipped entirely since no writes will occur. This saves memory and CPU for large reads. Some JPA providers also use this hint to route queries to read replicas. For optimistic locking, @Version adds a version column to the entity table. On every UPDATE, Hibernate adds AND version = :currentVersion to the WHERE clause. If another transaction committed a concurrent update, the version in the database is higher than what we loaded — the WHERE clause finds no rows, row count is 0, Hibernate detects this and throws OptimisticLockingFailureException. This prevents the 'lost update' problem without database-level locks, enabling high concurrency. Optimistic locking is ideal for low-contention scenarios; use pessimistic locking (@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)) for high-contention scenarios.

methodSignatures.description: Marks a Long/int field as the optimistic lock version; auto-incremented on each UPDATE
Performance hint: skips dirty checking; used for pure read methods
Thrown when the version check fails, indicating a concurrent modification

title: EntityGraph on a Repository Method
description: Define a @NamedEntityGraph on the Order entity that eagerly loads the customer and each item's product. Apply this graph to a repository method using @EntityGraph. Also implement a Slice-based paginated query for orders.
hints: @NamedEntityGraph(name='...', attributeNodes={@NamedAttributeNode(value='items', subgraph='sub')}, subgraphs={@NamedSubgraph(name='sub', attributeNodes=@NamedAttributeNode('product'))})
@EntityGraph('Order.withCustomerAndDetails') on the repository method references the named graph
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {'customer'}) for inline attribute paths
Slice<Order> findByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc(OrderStatus status, Pageable pageable) for the Slice query

solution.explanation: @NamedEntityGraph on the entity class defines a reusable fetch plan. The subgraph feature allows deep loading: items are loaded as part of the order, and each item's product is loaded as part of the items subgraph — all in a single SQL query with two JOINs. @EntityGraph on the repository method applies the graph to that specific query without modifying the entity's default fetching behavior. The FETCH type (default) means unspecified attributes remain LAZY. Inline attributePaths on @EntityGraph is simpler for ad-hoc cases without defining a @NamedEntityGraph. Slice<T> is the right choice when you don't need total count (e.g., infinite scroll) — it fires only one query (no COUNT *), while Page<T> fires two. Spring MVC automatically binds Pageable from request params: ?page=0&size=10&sort=createdAt,desc.

methodSignatures.description: Defines a reusable load plan on the entity class; referenced by name in @EntityGraph
Applies an entity graph to a specific repository method
Returns a slice of results without total count; no COUNT query fired

title: Auditable Base Class with @MappedSuperclass
description: Create an Auditable @MappedSuperclass with @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy fields. Configure JPA auditing in a @Configuration class with a custom AuditorAware bean that reads the username from Spring SecurityContextHolder.
hints: @MappedSuperclass means the fields are included in subclasses but Auditable itself has no table
@CreatedDate on LocalDateTime createdAt — @Column(updatable = false) to prevent accidental updates
AuditorAware<String> returns Optional<String>; return Optional.of(username) or Optional.of('system')
Read from SecurityContextHolder: SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName()

solution.explanation: @MappedSuperclass instructs JPA to map the superclass fields into the subclass table — there is no 'auditable' table. @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class) hooks the entity into Spring Data's auditing events (pre-persist and pre-update). @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate work with LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Instant, Long, or java.util.Date. @Column(updatable = false) on createdAt prevents accidental updates to the creation timestamp. The AuditorAware lambda reads the current user from Spring Security; the AnonymousAuthenticationToken check handles unauthenticated requests (batch jobs, scheduled tasks) gracefully by using 'system' as the auditor. @EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef) wires the custom bean — without this, @CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy fields remain null.

methodSignatures.description: Fields are included in subclass tables; the superclass itself has no table
Required for Spring Data auditing to work; hooks pre-persist/pre-update events
Enables auditing; auditorAwareRef points to the AuditorAware bean name

title: JPQL with GROUP BY, HAVING, and Projections
description: Write JPQL queries that use aggregation: find departments with average salary above a threshold, return results as a DTO using constructor expression. Also write a query that finds employees with the highest salary in each department.
hints: SELECT new com.app.dto.DepartmentSalaryDto(e.department, AVG(e.salary), COUNT(e)) FROM Employee e GROUP BY e.department HAVING AVG(e.salary) > :min
The DTO constructor parameters must match the SELECT expressions in type and order
For max salary per dept: SELECT e.department, MAX(e.salary) FROM Employee e GROUP BY e.department
Correlated subquery: WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM Employee e2 WHERE e2.department = e.department)

solution.explanation: The constructor expression NEW ClassName(...) in JPQL is the cleanest way to map aggregation results to DTOs without returning Object[]. JPA calls the matching constructor with the aggregated values. The full package name is required in the constructor expression. HAVING filters groups after aggregation — it's the JPQL equivalent of SQL's HAVING clause. AVG() and COUNT() in HAVING must match the expressions in SELECT exactly. Correlated subqueries in JPQL work the same as SQL: the inner query references the outer query's alias (e.department = e.department — outer 'e' refers to the outer query's Employee). Correlated subqueries can be slow on large tables; an alternative is to join the Employee table to a subquery, but JPQL doesn't support that — use native SQL or Criteria API for that case.

methodSignatures.description: Constructor expression: JPQL calls Dto(expr1, expr2) constructor for each result row
Filters groups after aggregation; can reference aggregate functions
Inner subquery references outer query's alias; evaluated once per outer row

title: CascadeType Strategy for Different Relationships
description: Design a Blog domain with three entity relationships that need different cascade strategies: Post → Comments (comments are owned by post), Post → Tags (tags are shared entities), and User → Posts (posts belong to user). Choose appropriate cascade types and orphanRemoval for each. Explain your reasoning.
hints: Comments are 'owned' by Post — use CascadeType.ALL + orphanRemoval = true
Tags are independent entities shared by multiple posts — deleting a Post should NOT delete a Tag
For Tags: CascadeType.PERSIST, CascadeType.MERGE only — so you can create new tags with a post, but deleting a post doesn't delete tags
For User → Posts: think about what happens when a user is deleted. Should all their posts be deleted? Usually yes → CascadeType.ALL

solution.explanation: Cascade type selection is a business decision, not a technical default. Ask: 'If the parent disappears, should the children disappear?' For Comments: yes — a comment without a post is orphaned data, so CascadeType.ALL + orphanRemoval = true. For Tags: no — a Tag is an independent entity used by many posts; deleting a Post should only remove the join table row, not the Tag itself. CascadeType.PERSIST + MERGE allows creating and updating tags alongside posts without accidentally deleting them. For User → Posts: this is a judgment call. If your business rules say 'deleting a user deletes all their content', use CascadeType.ALL. If posts should be preserved with an anonymous/deleted user attribution, don't cascade REMOVE — just null the author FK. Never blindly use CascadeType.ALL; always reason through each cascade operation.

methodSignatures.description: Propagates all operations (PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, DETACH, REFRESH) to child entities
Safe for shared entities — allows saving new and merging existing without deleting
Delete child when removed from parent's collection; requires owning entity to have the collection

title: Pagination and Sorting API Endpoint
description: Implement a paginated product search REST endpoint. The endpoint accepts page, size, sortBy, sortDir, and an optional nameFilter query parameter. Use Spring Data's Pageable and return a Page<ProductDto> with metadata (totalElements, totalPages, currentPage).
hints: @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = 'name') Pageable pageable as a method parameter — Spring MVC auto-binds page, size, sort params
productRepo.findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(nameFilter, pageable) if filter is not blank; otherwise findAll(pageable)
page.map(product -> productMapper.toDto(product)) converts Page<Product> to Page<ProductDto>
Use Sort.by(Sort.Direction.fromString(sortDir), sortBy) for dynamic sort direction

solution.explanation: @PageableDefault provides defaults so callers don't need to always specify pagination params. Spring MVC maps ?page=0&size=10&sort=name,asc to a PageRequest automatically. The sort parameter supports multiple sort criteria: ?sort=price,desc&sort=name,asc. page.map() is the clean way to transform a Page<Entity> into a Page<DTO> — it preserves all pagination metadata (totalElements, totalPages, number, size) while replacing the content. @Transactional(readOnly = true) is important here — it skips Hibernate's dirty checking overhead for what is purely a read operation. The Page<ProductDto> response body Jackson serializes includes content (the list), totalElements, totalPages, size, and number — everything a frontend needs to build a pagination UI.

methodSignatures.description: Sets default pagination values; Spring MVC overrides with request parameters
Transforms page content while preserving pagination metadata
Returns a Page<T> with the content, total count, and pagination info

title: Diagnose and Fix LazyInitializationException
description: Given code that throws LazyInitializationException, identify why it happens and implement three different fixes: (1) @Transactional on the service method, (2) JOIN FETCH query, (3) DTO projection that avoids lazy loading entirely.
hints: Fix 1: @Transactional(readOnly = true) keeps the session open for the entire method
Fix 2: @Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer JOIN FETCH o.items WHERE o.id = :id") in repository
Fix 3: @Query("SELECT new com.app.OrderSummary(o.id, o.customer.name, SIZE(o.items)) FROM Order o JOIN o.customer WHERE o.id = :id")
Fix 3 is the best for production — no entity loading, no lazy proxies, returns only what you need

solution.explanation: LazyInitializationException has one root cause: accessing a lazy proxy after the Hibernate session (persistence context) is closed. Fix 1 is the simplest but least efficient — @Transactional keeps the session alive, but you may still fire multiple SQL queries for each lazy access. Fix 2 (JOIN FETCH) is better for performance — one SQL query loads everything. Fix 3 (DTO projection) is the gold standard for APIs: you never load entities or proxies at all, only the data you need. The constructor expression fires a single optimized SQL query and returns a plain object — no proxy, no session dependency, no risk of additional lazy loads. Disable spring.jpa.open-in-view=false in production to force yourself to use Fix 2 or 3; OSIV masks this problem at the cost of open database connections throughout the HTTP request.

methodSignatures.description: Keeps persistence context alive for the method duration; use as a baseline fix
Loads association eagerly in one SQL JOIN; prevents additional SELECT queries
Returns a plain DTO object directly from JPQL; no entity proxy created, no lazy loading possible

title: Entity Lifecycle and Dirty Checking
description: Interview question: Explain the JPA entity lifecycle states (NEW, MANAGED, DETACHED, REMOVED) and how dirty checking works. Why do you NOT need to call save() to update a managed entity?
hints: What does 'managed' mean in terms of the persistence context?
When does Hibernate flush/sync changes to the database?
What is the snapshot Hibernate takes when loading an entity?

solution.explanation: Dirty checking is one of JPA's most powerful and misunderstood features. It is Hibernate's mechanism for tracking changes to managed entities and generating appropriate SQL at flush time. The persistence context maintains a first-level identity map (entity cache) and a snapshot of each entity's state when it was loaded. At flush time, Hibernate compares current state to snapshots and generates UPDATE SQL for any modified entities. This is why @Transactional is essential for update operations — without it, the entity is detached as soon as the repository method returns, and no automatic dirty checking occurs. Understanding the four states is fundamental to debugging JPA issues: most 'why wasn't my data saved?' bugs come from modifying DETACHED entities.

title: First-Level vs Second-Level Cache
description: Interview question: What is the difference between the first-level cache (L1) and second-level cache (L2) in Hibernate/JPA? What are the L1 guarantees? When would you use L2 cache and what are the risks?
hints: L1 is always on; L2 is optional and explicit
L1 is per EntityManager/Session (per transaction); L2 is per EntityManagerFactory (shared)
L2 cache risks: stale data when updates bypass JPA (native SQL, another app instance)

solution.explanation: The L1 cache (persistence context) is a fundamental part of JPA's object identity guarantee — within a transaction, you always get the same Java object for the same entity ID. This is the first-level cache. The L2 cache is an application-wide cache that persists between transactions, dramatically reducing database load for reference data. However, it introduces consistency challenges: bypassing JPA (native SQL, external tools, other microservices) can leave the L2 cache stale. The most common L2 cache mistake is enabling it for entities that are frequently updated or modified by external processes. A simpler alternative for many cases: Spring's @Cacheable on service methods, which is easier to reason about and invalidate.

title: Flush Modes and When Hibernate Syncs to DB
description: Interview question: What is a flush in Hibernate? What are the flush modes (AUTO, COMMIT, MANUAL, ALWAYS)? When does Hibernate flush? What happens if you query after modifying a managed entity but before the transaction commits?
hints: FlushModeType.AUTO flushes before queries to maintain consistency within the transaction
The UPDATE is not issued immediately after setPrice() — it's deferred to flush time
With AUTO mode, Hibernate detects that the pending Product change could affect the findByPriceGreaterThan query and flushes first

solution.explanation: Understanding flush modes is critical for understanding JPA's transactional behavior. The AUTO flush mode is designed to maintain read-your-own-writes consistency within a transaction — if you modify an entity and then query the same table, you'll see your own modifications in the query results because Hibernate flushes before the query. This is the default and almost always what you want. COMMIT mode trades consistency for performance — useful in batch processing where you know queries won't be affected by pending changes. The key interview insight: SQL is generated lazily and batched by default; Hibernate defers DML as long as possible (until query time with AUTO, or until commit) to enable query optimization and reduce round trips.

title: N+1 Problem — Identify and Fix
description: Interview question: What is the N+1 query problem in JPA? Give a concrete example with numbers. What are three different ways to fix it, and when would you choose each approach?
hints: N+1 = 1 query for parents + N separate queries for each child association
Solution 1: JOIN FETCH — loads in a single SQL JOIN
Solution 2: @EntityGraph — declarative alternative to JOIN FETCH
Solution 3: DTO projection — don't load entities at all

solution.explanation: The N+1 problem is the most common JPA performance issue and a standard interview topic. The root cause is LAZY loading combined with iteration: each iteration triggers a separate SELECT for the lazy association. The 'N' is the number of parent records; even a small table with 50 rows can generate 51 queries. For a large table with 10,000 rows, this is catastrophic. Fix selection: JOIN FETCH for flexible queries where you need full entities; @EntityGraph for declarative per-method overrides; DTO projection for reporting and API endpoints where you only need specific fields. The DTO approach is the most performant because it loads only required columns and avoids entity object creation overhead. Always enable SQL logging in development and audit query counts — one endpoint firing 101 queries is a bug, not a feature.

title: Persistence Context and Transaction Scope
description: Interview question: What is the persistence context in JPA? What is its default scope in a Spring application? What happens to entities when the persistence context closes, and how does this lead to common bugs?
hints: In Spring, the default persistence context scope is per-transaction (transaction-scoped)
After @Transactional method returns, the persistence context is closed and entities become DETACHED
Two common bugs: LazyInitializationException and 'lost updates' when modifying detached entities

solution.explanation: The persistence context is JPA's unit-of-work container. Understanding its transaction-scoped lifecycle in Spring is the key to understanding most JPA bugs. The lifecycle: open at transaction start, track all loaded entities, flush at transaction end, close context after commit, leaving all entities DETACHED. DETACHED entities behave like regular Java objects — no tracking, no lazy loading. The two most common consequences are LazyInitializationException (accessing lazy proxy on detached entity) and silent data loss (modifying a detached entity without saving it). The inverse bug — unintended updates — happens when developers forget that loaded entities within @Transactional are MANAGED and any modification will trigger an UPDATE without an explicit save() call.
